query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase face-centered-cubic (FCC) high-entropy alloys, room-temperature hardness and yield strength scale primarily with the magnitude of atomic-size–mismatch lattice distortion (quantified by the misfit parameter δ); larger δ produces a roughly linear increase in hardness (≈ +15–25 Vickers per 1 at.% increase in δ) until the distortion exceeds ≈6 %, at which point secondary phases nucleate and the solid-solution hardening effect saturates or is partially lost.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenised, recrystallised equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with grain size >10 µm and a single-phase FCC structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically substitute one larger-radius element (e.g., Al or Ti) for one base element in 0–10 at.% increments to tune δ while keeping total valence electron concentration roughly constant and avoiding precipitation heat treatments.
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical testing; grain size maintained >10 µm; no intentional cold work or aging; anneal just above recrystallisation temperature to ensure single-phase FCC before testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Static local lattice distortion fields surrounding solute atoms, which increase the Peierls stress for dislocation glide.
generation.mechanism: Greater atomic-size misfit produces larger local strain fields that interact elastically with moving dislocations, increasing the force required for glide (solid-solution strengthening). Once δ exceeds ~6 %, elastic strain energy drives chemical partitioning and formation of secondary phases, consuming solute atoms and relaxing the lattice distortion, so additional strengthening ceases or reverses.
generation.predicted_outcome: For samples that remain single-phase FCC, Vickers hardness and 0.2 % offset yield strength will rise monotonically with δ, approximately 15–25 HV and 40–60 MPa per 1 % increase in δ. When δ surpasses ~6 %, X-ray diffraction will reveal new phases and the hardness/strength will plateau or drop below the linear extrapolation.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (δ ≈0.8 %) is expected to show ~160 HV and ~400 MPa yield strength under the stated conditions.
generation.boundary: Applies to FCC HEAs with grain size above the Hall–Petch saturation regime (>10 µm), tested at 20–30 °C, in the absence of significant short-range order, precipitation, or martensitic transformation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact numerical slope of hardness vs. δ and the critical δ for phase separation may vary with processing history and specific solute choice; stacking-fault energy changes could introduce secondary effects not captured here.

falsification_experiment.design: Cast a series of CoCrFeMnNi-xAl alloys with x = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 at.%; homogenise at 1100 °C/24 h, cold roll 80 %, anneal at 900 °C/1 h, air cool. Measure compositions to compute δ, verify single-phase FCC by XRD/EBSD, then perform nanoindentation and uniaxial tensile tests.
measurements: Composition and δ for each alloy
0.2 % offset yield strength from tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, for alloys that remain single-phase FCC (no secondary peaks in XRD), hardness or yield strength does not increase monotonically with δ within experimental scatter (±5 %) or if alloys with δ >6 % but still single-phase do not deviate from the linear trend.
